birth.stop: Lauingen on the Danube, the birth
birth.date_confidence: The year is not documented. German scholarship quotes Weisheipl to the effect that nothing more can be said than that Albert was born around 1200 or somewhat earlier; Italian reference works give a range between 1193 and 1206; the Linda Hall Library states flatly that his date of birth is not known. New Advent's 1205 or 1206 is one conjecture among several. Set to 1200-01-01 to open the file. The Lauingen association itself is attested only through the byname, Albertus de Lauingen.

stops.stop: Cologne, the testament
stops.date_confidence: Sources conflict on the year and the conflict is flagged rather than resolved. January 1279 is adopted here, with 1278 recorded as the competing reading. The detail about the choir exceeding mendicant building norms comes from the dossier and was not checked against a transcription of the will.

stops.stop: Cologne, the memory goes
stops.date_confidence: The decline is reported (English Wikipedia, '1278 - Health declined'; New Advent, 'Some time after 1278... he suffered a lapse of memory') and presented in both as ordinary aging, not as a fulfilled prophecy. The Kierkegaard line is quoted here from the English Wikipedia article; Kierkegaard's own text was not fetched. Date set between the testament and the death.

stops.segment: The Testament, the Grave, and the Legends
stops.stop: Cologne, death in the cell
stops.date_confidence: Attested: New Advent, 'died at Cologne, 15 November 1280', corroborated by the Stanford Encyclopedia and by Wikipedia. That he died sitting in his cell at the convent of the Holy Cross follows the Vatican general audience of 24 March 2010; that dedication is more specific than the plain 'Dominican convent' used in the other sources, and the discrepancy in naming is noted rather than resolved. No cause of death is named anywhere consulted.

stops.stop: Cologne, buried in the choir
stops.date_confidence: Burial in the choir of the Dominican church is attested by New Advent and corroborated in the standard modern treatments. The date of the funeral is not recorded anywhere consulted; 17 November is set two days after the death purely to order the file. The near-contemporary praise quoted here is by his own pupil Ulrich Engelbert; note that some chronologies attribute the sentence to the Stanford Encyclopedia, which does not contain it.

stops.segment: The Testament, the Grave, and the Legends
stops.stop: Rome, patron of the natural sciences
stops.date_confidence: 1941 is attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia, 'made patron saint of natural scientists in 1941 by Pius XII', and by the Vatican general audience of 24 March 2010. Month and day unknown. The Albertus-Magnus-Institut's own site confirms its 1931 founding, its Bonn location under the Archdiocese of Cologne, and the Editio Coloniensis as its purpose, but gives neither the edition's start year nor its volume count; the commonly cited 1951 is therefore not asserted here. Jammy's Lyon edition of 1651 in 21 folio volumes and Borgnet's Paris edition of 1890-1899 in 38 are attested.

stops.segment: The Testament, the Grave, and the Legends
stops.stop: Saint Andreas, Cologne: the Roman sarcophagus
stops.date_confidence: The relics at Saint Andreas and the third-century Roman sarcophagus are attested by the English Wikipedia article on the church, whose coordinates 50.9417 / 6.9539 are used exactly. The transfer date is contested and is left contested: German Wikipedia's Albert article says the bones have rested there since the suppression of the convent in 1804, while its article on the Cologne Dominican convent dates the transfer to 1802, with the church closed 28 September 1802 and demolished in 1804. Read as 1802-1804. The 1954 installation in the sarcophagus comes from the dossier alone, is not independently confirmed, and is used here only as the stop's date.
